Meta-Analysis of Genome-Wide Association Studies of Human Milk Oligosaccharide Composition

Author

Uma Agarwal Mentor: Kelsey Johnson, PhD

Introduction:

Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) are the third most abundant non-water compounds of human milk, following lactose and lipids. While not directly metabolized by the infant, HMOs are bioactive components of breast milk that contribute to infant nutrition, immune development, and microbiome composition.

Several distinct HMO structures have been identified, all of which originate from lactose; they are catalyzed by a variety of different enzymes to add various functional groups, such as fucose, sialic acid, or N-acetylglucosamine. Notable, the FUT2 enzyme catalyzes the alpha-1,2 addition of fucose to lactose to produce 2’-fucosyllactose (2’FL).

Milk from a single lactating mother can contain 12-20 distinct HMOs in varying concentrations. Understanding the maternal genetic determinants of HMO composition may improve understanding of lactation biology and inter-individual variation in milk composition.

To our knowledge, to date there have been no meta-analyses conducted to examine the genetic associations of HMO composition in human milk. Analyses of the genetics behind HMO composition in individual cohorts suffer from small sample sizes and low statistical power, potentially obscuring real associations. Here, we aim to utilize meta-analysis pipelines to improve statistical power and reveal further genetic associations with HMO composition in human milk.

Methods:

Genome-wide association summary-level statistics from three independent cohorts: MILK study (n=540), CHILD study (n=980), and Dutch Lifelines NEXT cohort (n=524), were harmonized in preparation for meta-analysis. Summary statistics from CHILD and Lifelines were each converted from genomic build GRCh37 (hg19) to GRCh38 (hg38) using UCSC’s command-line tool LiftOver. Additionally, all variants were renamed across all three cohorts for consistency, and variants for which the beta values, standard errors, and/or p-values were missing were removed.

For the meta-analysis of all cohorts, METAL was used. METAL’s SCHEME STDERR was used to produce effect size estimates of each variant across all cohorts. Additionally, the ANALYZE HETEROGENEITY option was used to produce heterogeneity statistics across all cohorts. Sample sizes and allele frequencies were specified to METAL to allow for accurate effect size weightage.

Two meta-analysis pipelines were run: one in which phenotypes shared by all three cohorts were meta-analyzed, and a second run in which additional phenotypes shared by only the MILK and CHILD cohorts were meta-analyzed. There were no phenotypes shared only by the MILK and Lifelines cohorts. Across the MILK, CHILD, and Lifelines cohorts, thirteen HMO phenotypes were analyzed, plus three additional summary-level phenotypes. Across the MILK and CHILD cohorts, six additional phenotypes were meta-analyzed (Figure 1).

Post-analysis summary tables were constructed in R using the data.table and tidyverse package libraries. Forest plots were constructed in R using ggplot2, and QQplots and Manhattan plots additionally used the qqman library. Locuszoom plots were constructed in R using the locuszoomr, ensembldb, EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75 libraries.

Results:

Figure 1 shows the shared phenotypes across the MILK, CHILD, and Lifelines cohorts, as well as those shared by only the MILK and CHILD cohorts.

Meta-analysis of all three cohorts:

METAL processed 6320655 variants from the MILK cohort, 5470256 variants from the CHILD cohort, and 5378353 variants from the Lifelines cohort; from these, a total of 8100661 variants were finally meta-analyzed. Table 1 shows the genome-wide significant SNP variants (p-value < 5e-8) from all phenotypes meta-analyzed across all three cohorts, along with the effect-allele frequency (averaged across all three cohorts) and standard error, the meta-analyzed beta effect size and standard error, p-value, heterogeneity statistics (I-squared and Cochran’s Q p-value), and effect direction for each SNP variant. The large heterogeneity Q p-values suggest that there is little to no heterogeneity across cohorts, which reassures that the summary statistics across the three cohorts were correctly harmonized and that any relatedness or residual population structure within the cohorts has been appropriately controlled for. Figure 2 shows the overlayed Manhattan plot for all phenotypes included in this three-cohort meta-analysis. Figure 3 shows forest plots of the individual cohort beta effect sizes compared to the meta-analyzed beta effect size for each top SNP variant.

Among the top hits, seven different genetic loci were identified. Four of these loci (FUT2 at Chr19:48703417, FUT3/FUT6 at Chr19:5832198, ST6GAL1 at Chr3:187041559, and FAM3C at Chr7: 121541964) have been previously identified in individual-level GWAS analyses to be associated with HMO concentrations.

Three additional loci were found from the meta-analysis. The SNP variant at Chr4:41326544 was found to be associated with LNnT concentration. This region contains the LIMCH1 gene (Figure 4), which encodes a myosin II binding protein, which has been found to be involved in breast cancer biology and mammary cell epithelium.

knitr::include_graphics("results/all_cohorts/locus_plot_lnnt.png")

Additionally, the SNP variant at Chr17:7385193 was found to be associated with DSLNT concentration. This region contains the TNK1 gene (Figure 5), which encodes a non-receptor tyrosine kinase involved in intracellular signaling and cell growth. While this gene has not been previously identified in association with human milk biology, it has been previously identified in playing a role in milk production in donkeys.

knitr::include_graphics("results/all_cohorts/locus_plot_dslnt.png")

Finally, the SNP variant at Chr6:113224735 was found to be associated with DSLNT concentration. This region contains the SOCS5P5, which is a non-functional pseudogene derived from the SOCS5 gene. While the SOCS5 gene, which encodes a suppressor of cytokine signaling protein involved in immune response and mammary gland development, has been previously associated with milk production in cattle, it is unclear how the non-functional pseudogene is involved in milk biology or mammary gland physiology.

knitr::include_graphics("results/all_cohorts/locus_plot_dslnt_chr6.png")

Meta-analysis of MILK & CHILD cohorts:

In the meta-analysis of the MILK and CHILD cohorts only, METAL processed 6320655 variants from the MILK cohort and 5470256 variants from the CHILD cohort; from these, a total of 6320655 variants were finally meta-analyzed.

Table 2 shows the genome-wide significant (p-value < 5e-8) SNP variants from the phenotypes shared by these two cohorts. Once again, the large heterogeneity Q p-values suggest that there is little to no heterogeneity across cohorts, which reassures that the summary statistics across the three cohorts were correctly harmonized and that any relatedness or residual population structure within the cohorts has been appropriately controlled for. Figure 6 shows the overlayed Manhattan plot for the additional phenotypes covered by this two-cohort meta-analysis. Figure 7 shows forest plots of the individual cohort beta effect sizes compared to the meta-analyzed beta effect size for each top SNP variant.

From this secondary meta-analysis, one additional genetic locus was identified: the SNP variant at Chr15:59544557 was found to be associated with FLNH concentration. In this region, the GCNT3 gene, which encodes a N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase enzyme, can be found. This enzyme has been previously associated with milk production in humans.

Discussion & Limitations:

In this project, meta-analysis pipelines were utilized to improve statistical power and reveal novel genetic associations with HMO composition in human milk. By meta-analyzing summary-level GWAS statistics from three independent cohorts, eight total genetic loci were identified, 3 of which are believed to be novel in their associations with human milk biology.

Although meta-analysis substantially increased statistical power and enabled the identification of eight genetic loci associated with HMO composition, including three potentially novel loci, several limitations should be considered. First, the identified associations are statistical and do not establish causal relationships or identify the underlying causal variants or genes. At the time of this study, downstream functional analyses, such as fine-mapping, colocalization, expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analyses, transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS), or experimental validation, have not yet been performed. As a result, the biological mechanisms linking these loci to HMO biosynthesis remain unresolved.

Additionally, differences in cohort characteristics, sample sizes, and phenotype measurement protocols may have introduced residual heterogeneity despite the use of meta-analysis methods. Finally, because the study population was limited to the available cohorts, of which were primarily European ancestry, the generalizability of these findings to other ancestral populations remains to be determined. Future work incorporating functional genomics, experimental validation, and more diverse populations will be essential for confirming the causal genes and elucidating the biological pathways underlying these associations. Therefore, the novel loci reported here should be considered candidate regions for future investigation rather than definitive evidence of the genes or molecular pathways regulating HMO composition.
